newsitem.title: TURKEY: Islamist PM gets no aid from civilian leaders.
newsitem.headline: Islamist PM gets no aid from civilian leaders.

text.p: Turkey's politicians on Wednesday rebuffed pleas from Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan that the army was subverting democracy and demanded he toe the secularist line laid out by the generals.

"The prime minister said it was a time for solidarity to protect democracy and that he expected cooperation from us," main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz told reporters after talks with the prime minister.
"I told him we did not agree. I said it was up to him to clear up the problem," Yilmaz said. Three big labour unions and two leftist leaders earlier delivered a similar message.

The National Security Council, a constitutional body dominated by the military, demanded at the weekend that Erbakan's coalition crackdown on religious activism, which they say was largely fostered by his Islam-based Welfare party.
Erbakan has so far refused, arguing that democracy meant his government answered only to parliament, not to the army.
The beleagured prime minister met later with coalition partner Tansu Ciller, a pro-Western conservative, but he made no comment after brief talks.

The deadlock with the army, which has has ousted three civilian governments in 37 years, rattled financial markets and may threatens to further complicate Turkey's bid for closer European integration.

The Istanbul share index closed off 4.92 percent for the day, capping a decline of 14.9 percent since the Security Council warning. Bond yields were also up sharply on Wednesday, jumping 6-8 percentage points to around 110 percent.
Traders said markets were nervous that ambitious privatisation and budget targets would be lost in the political turmoil.
Ciller, who is also foreign minister, suggested the crisis could also damage its chances of joining the European club. She planned to lobby ambassadors from EU countries on Thursday.
"To be successful we need a continuation of stability," she told reporters. "The continuation of the secular Turkish republic and democracy are very important. A shadow should not be cast on them."
Long-held dreams of a place in the European Union received a public blow on Tuesday, when leading EU figures spoke out against Turkey's membership. It now has associate member status.

Turkey's three biggest trade unions, meanwhile, said the army's move to quell alleged Islamist separatism had the full support of their six million members. Leftist leaders told told Erbakan the same thing on Tuesday.

Mainstream newspapers and television channels have joined the chorus of approval for the NSC, with some even urging the army to topple the government. Nightly street demonstrations have increasingly targetted the Islamists.
This groundswell behind the military chiefs reflects widespread respect for the armed forces among Turkey's secular majority as a bulwark against religious extremism.
"Modern, secular democracy is in danger," said the chiefs of three big unions in a joint letter to party leaders. "This is why we support the National Security Council decisions."
The mass-circulation Hurriyet daily quoted Ridvan Budak, chairmen of the leftist union DISK, as saying civilians must now follow the lead of the soldiers.
"The Turkish armed forces have done their duty, now it is the task of civilian authority...The regime is in danger," Budak said.
